Liar
LY-er
n.
From lie, Old English leogan, to speak falsely. Webster 1828: one who knowingly utters falsehood. In Scripture the noun is used with unusual force: of every man over against God, of the devil as the father of lies, and of the professor whose life contradicts his claim to know Christ.

Biblical Definition

Scripture uses liar to settle three questions. First, who is truthful when God and man disagree: let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings (Romans 3:4). Where a man’s account and God’s account conflict, the verdict is fixed in advance. Second, the origin of falsehood: our Lord tells the religious leaders of their father the devil, When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it (John 8:44). Lying is not a lapse in the devil’s case but his native speech. Third, and most searchingly, the test of profession: He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him (1 John 2:4), and If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us (1 John 1:10). John will not permit a Christianity of claims. Proverbs adds the ordinary wisdom — a poor man is better than a liar (Proverbs 19:22), and Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar (Proverbs 30:6), which makes adding to Scripture a species of lying.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LIAR as one who knowingly utters falsehood; one who declares to another as a fact what he knows to be not true. The knowledge is essential: a man mistaken is not thereby a liar.

expand to see more

LIAR, n. — A person who knowingly utters falsehood; one who declares to another as a fact what he knows to be not true, and with an intention to deceive him.

One who tells lies habitually; a person given to falsehood.

Webster’s insistence on knowledge and intention matters pastorally. Scripture’s hardest uses of the noun — John 8:44, 1 John 2:4 — are not applied to the mistaken but to those whose profession and practice knowingly diverge.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 30:6 — "Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar."

John 8:44 — "Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it."

Romans 3:4 — "God forbid: yea, let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged."

1 John 1:10 — "If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us."

1 John 2:4 — "He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him."

Modern Corruption

The word is corrupted wherever truth is treated as a matter of perspective, so that no one can be a liar in the strict sense; and it is evaded wherever a profession of faith is allowed to stand against a contradicting life, which 1 John 2:4 refuses.

expand to see more

Romans 3:4 is the verse that decides the question of whose account governs. Paul is arguing that God’s faithfulness is not overthrown by human unbelief, and he settles it with a fixed rule: let God be true, but every man a liar. That sentence is unavailable to any framework in which truth is constructed by communities or measured by a speaker’s standpoint. If truth is perspectival, then no one lies; there are only competing accounts. Scripture treats falsehood as a real relation between what is said and what is, and it treats God’s word as the fixed term against which every human account is measured.

1 John 2:4 is the harder application, and it is aimed at the church rather than the world. He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar — not weak, not immature, not on a journey, but a liar, and the truth is not in him. John is not teaching justification by obedience; the same letter says that if any man sin we have an advocate with the Father. He is teaching that a profession which produces no obedience is a false statement about oneself. Proverbs 30:6 makes the corresponding warning about Scripture itself: to add to God’s words is to be found a liar, which is why the closed canon and the sufficiency of Scripture are not dry doctrines but matters of honesty.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew nouns are from roots for deception and vanity; the Greek pseustes is the standing New Testament term, used of the devil, of the false professor, and of every man over against God.

expand to see more

Hebrew kazab (H3576) — to lie, to be found a liar; lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar (Proverbs 30:6).

Hebrew 'akzab (H391) — deceptive, failing; the figure of waters that fail in Jeremiah 15:18.

Greek pseustes (G5583) — a liar; John 8:44, Romans 3:4, 1 John 1:10 and 2:4.

Greek pseudos (G5579) — a lie, falsehood; the devil speaks of his own when he speaks it.

Revelation 21:8 places all liars in the list of those whose part is in the lake of fire, which measures how seriously Scripture takes the noun.

Usage

"Let God be true, but every man a liar (Romans 3:4) — the fixed verdict when God’s account and man’s conflict."

"He is a liar, and the father of it (John 8:44) — falsehood traced to its origin."

"He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar (1 John 2:4) — profession tested by obedience."
